summary: For ages 7–9: learners come to understand rainforest plant adaptations as structures that solve specific environmental problems (too wet, too dark, too thin-soiled) — drip-tip leaves shed water to prevent rot, wide shallow buttress roots brace tall trees in thin soil, epiphytes perch high on branches to reach light without soil, and lianas climb other trunks to reach the canopy cheaply. The core activities use predict-then-reveal cause-and-effect (what fails without the adaptation, what succeeds with it), and learners repeatedly use the umbrella term 'adaptation' to mean an inherited survival feature. Supporting activities offer an annotated reference tree and matching/labelling for recall.
misconceptions: 'Epiphytes are parasites stealing food from the tree' — they only perch for a light-rich position; they make their own food.
'Buttress roots go deep' — they spread WIDE and shallow because the nutrient/anchor layer is thin.
'Drip-tips are just a leaf shape' — they serve a purpose: shedding water to prevent rot and fungal growth.
'Lianas are tree trunks' — they are climbers using other trees for support to reach light cheaply.
'Adaptation means the plant tried/chose to change' — adaptations are inherited features, not deliberate acts.

activities.title: Rainforest plant repair workshop: switch each adaptation on and off
steps: Before testing, predict: what would happen to a broad, flat, tip-less leaf sitting under constant rainforest rain?

Pour (or simulate) rain onto a flat, tip-less leaf and watch how water sits on it; then shape a pointed drip-tip and watch the water collect and run off the tip faster. (In a real rainforest, a leaf that stays wet for a long time is more likely to grow mould or rot; a short demonstration will not show rotting.) State in one sentence the problem the drip-tip solves.

Give a tall model tree ordinary narrow roots on a thin layer of soil and push it gently: it topples easily. Then unfold wide buttress flanges at its base and push again: it stays upright much better. State why wide (not deep) roots help here.

Compare an epiphyte seedling (such as an orchid) on the dark forest floor, where it gets too little light to make enough food and grows poorly, with the same kind of seedling perched high on a branch, where it reaches the light and can grow and flower. State the problem the high position solves.
Show a liana climbing an existing trunk toward the canopy instead of building its own thick trunk, and say why climbing is a cheaper route to the light.
For each test, read or write a one-line 'problem solved' caption pairing the STRUCTURE with the PROBLEM.
activities.insight: Each strange plant feature is an ANSWER to a specific rainforest problem: too wet (drip-tip), a tall tree in thin soil (buttress), too dark below (epiphyte height, liana climbing). Structure→function becomes something the learner has seen cause and effect for, not just memorised.

activities.title: One annotated rainforest tree: tap each adaptation to its purpose
steps: Explore a single hero rainforest tree with drip-tip leaves and buttress roots, plus two separate plants growing on it: an epiphyte perched on a branch and a liana climbing the trunk.
Tap or reveal each hotspot to find the problem it solves (e.g. drip-tip → constant rain would rot a flat leaf, so the point drains it fast).
Tie each adaptation to the forest LAYER that matters: darkness is the problem near the floor, so epiphytes and lianas get up to the light in the canopy; buttresses anchor the tree at the floor.
activities.insight: A single reference tree shows all four structure→purpose pairings together and anchors them to the forest layers, giving learners a clear mental map to return to.

activities.title: Contrast and consolidate: rainforest solution vs a familiar plant
steps: Compare a rainforest plant with a familiar one (a daisy or an oak) and say what is different and why (e.g. an oak in deep British soil does not need wide buttress flanges).
Answer: would a tree still need wide buttress roots if the soil were deep and rich like a British field? Explain.
Match each adaptation to its purpose, and label a blank tree with drip-tip, buttress, epiphyte and liana in the right places.

Explain how two adaptations solve the SAME problem in different ways (e.g. epiphytes and lianas both solve 'too dark near the floor': epiphytes by perching high on branches, lianas by climbing trunks).
activities.insight: Contrasting with a familiar plant makes the rainforest solution stand out, and matching/labelling checks that the structure→purpose pairings are secured and transferable.

checkQuestion: A giant rainforest tree has huge 'buttress' roots that spread out sideways above the ground like fins. You might expect a tall tree to send roots DEEP down instead. Why do these roots spread WIDE across the surface rather than going deep? Tell me why, and then tell me what would go wrong if they grew deep instead.
checkAnswer: Because rainforest soil is thin and the goodness (nutrients) is all near the surface, so there's nothing to anchor into deep down. Wide buttress roots spread out over the surface both to hold up the huge tree AND to catch nutrients where they actually are — in the top layer. Deep roots would reach only poor, thin soil and wouldn't support or feed the tree well.
